topic: Astronomy is one of the oldest sciences, rooted in calendars, religion and astrology; the Babylonians kept systematic records from about 1000 BC.
Greek astronomers built geometric models of the heavens; Ptolemy's Earth-centred system in the 'Almagest' lasted 1,400 years.
Islamic astronomers refined it with better observations; Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo and Newton replaced it with a Sun-centred system governed by gravity.
From the 19th century, photography and spectroscopy revealed the stars' composition; the 20th century found galaxies, the expanding universe and the Big Bang.

Prehistory: Carvings and cave paintings may show star patterns: a 32,500-year-old mammoth tusk may depict Orion.
Monuments such as Stonehenge and the Goseck Circle are aligned with the Sun at the solstices.
The Nebra sky disc (about 1600 BC) is the oldest known realistic depiction of the sky.
Mesopotamia: Mesopotamian priests treated the heavens as signs from the gods, the origin of astrology.
Babylonians kept records of the sky for centuries and could predict lunar eclipses and planetary positions mathematically.
They divided the zodiac into 12 signs of 30 degrees, using their base-60 numbers.
India: Indian astronomy began with calendars; the Vedanga Jyotisha is the oldest astronomical text.
Aryabhata (499) proposed that the Earth rotates on its axis.
Brahmagupta and Bhāskara II developed mathematical astronomy.
Greece and Hellenistic world: Greeks treated astronomy as geometry; Eudoxus modelled planetary motion with nested spheres around the Earth.
Aristarchus proposed that the Earth goes round the Sun; Eratosthenes measured Earth's circumference.
Hipparchus catalogued stars, discovered the precession of the equinoxes and founded trigonometry.
The Antikythera mechanism (about 100 BC) was a geared calculator of astronomical positions.
Ptolemaic system: Ptolemy's 'Almagest' (about 150) set out an Earth-centred system with epicycles and deferents.
It predicted planetary positions well enough to be used until the Renaissance.
It was translated into Arabic and then Latin, shaping astronomy in both worlds.
Egypt: Egyptians aligned their calendar and monuments to the heliacal rising of Sirius, which heralded the Nile flood.
Pyramids and temples were aligned with the cardinal directions and with stars.
China: Chinese astronomers kept detailed records from about the 6th century BC.
They recorded comets, novae, sunspots and the supernova of 1054 (which formed the Crab Nebula).
Gan De and Shi Shen compiled early star catalogues; they could predict eclipses.
Mesoamerica: Maya astronomers tracked the cycles of the Sun, Moon, Venus and other planets.
The Dresden Codex contains tables predicting eclipses and the appearances of Venus.
Their calendars combined a 260-day ritual cycle with a 365-day year.
Middle Ages: Islamic astronomers translated Greek and Indian works, built observatories (Maragheh, Samarkand) and made precise observations.
Al-Sufi's 'Book of Fixed Stars' (964) described the Andromeda galaxy; Ibn al-Haytham and al-Tusi criticised Ptolemy.
Supernova SN 1006 was recorded across the world.
Western Europe relearned Greek astronomy from Arabic translations; the Alfonsine tables (1252) were used for centuries.
Renaissance and Early Modern Europe: Copernicus's 'De revolutionibus' (1543) placed the Sun at the centre.
Tycho Brahe made the most accurate naked-eye observations; Kepler used them to find that planets move in ellipses (1609).
Galileo's telescope (1610) showed Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus, supporting Copernicus; the Church condemned him in 1633.
Newton's 'Principia' (1687) explained planetary motion by universal gravitation; Uranus (1781) and Neptune (1846) were discovered.
Modern astronomy: Photography (from 1840) and spectroscopy (from Fraunhofer) revealed the stars' composition and motion.
The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram (about 1910) classified stars and led to theories of stellar evolution.
Hubble showed that other galaxies exist (1924) and that the universe is expanding (1929); the Big Bang theory was confirmed by the cosmic background radiation (1965).
Space telescopes, radio astronomy and probes, along with exoplanets (1995) and gravitational waves (2015), have transformed the field.
